coachMessages.text: Four green discs shaped like the letter J — and note the gap: the fourth column holds green on the first and third rows, not a stacked pair. Where could Green finish four-in-a-row from here?

slides.infoProse:
Green's four ringed discs form the letter J. Read them from the bottom: one disc at the foot of the fourth column, on the first row. Above it comes a gap — Gray owns the second row there. Then the shape closes: green discs side by side on the third row of the fourth and fifth columns, with one more green disc tucked underneath on the fifth column's second row.

Two things make this a J and not just a cluster. First, the gap column: the J's own column holds green discs on the first and third rows with one cell between them — it is not a stacked pair. Second, the neighbouring column carries two green discs, one level with the gap and one level with the upper disc — the hook of the J. The gap cell itself can even belong to Gray, as it does here; the J never needs it.

This exact position is Allen's textbook example. With Gray to move, the solver scores every Gray reply as losing. The next slide shows where that power comes from.

slides._boardInstructions: Same board as slide 1 (KB canonical 3334434, solver-verified). This slide reveals the triple threat: F3 = c6r3 (0-ind 5,2), G3 = c7r3 (0-ind 6,2), G4 = c7r4 (0-ind 6,3). All three are MINOR (x) threats on the render ('Major threats: none'), so they are marked with neutral 'claim' dots, NOT tg — tg would fail the verifier (no reachable Green threat there yet). Mechanism per Allen verbatim: 'sooner or later Red must get either G3 or G4 … In either case, F3 becomes a major threat' — G3 completes the row-3 horizontal D3-E3-F3-G3, G4 completes the rising diagonal D1-E2-F3-G4 from the J's foot. F3 sits on row 3 (odd) — the triple is equivalent to ONE major odd-row threat. scr (Gray to move): -5 -3 -4 -5 -4 -5 -5.

coachMessages.text: Three completing cells spread over two columns. As the seventh column fills, Green must land on one of the stacked pair — and either one turns the sixth-column cell into a major threat. Gray cannot cover them all.

legendItems.label: Green's three completing cells — two columns

slides.infoProse:
Count Green's ways to finish. Three cells matter, spread across two columns: the sixth column's third row, and the seventh column's third and fourth rows. None of them is a major threat yet — each winning line still needs two cells — but together they form a trap with no exit.

Here is Allen's argument. When the seventh column eventually fills, the players take its cells in turn, so sooner or later Green must get either its third row or its fourth row. Either one is enough. If Green lands on the seventh column's third row, the sixth column's third-row cell now completes four along the third row. If Green lands on the seventh column's fourth row instead, that same sixth-column cell completes the rising diagonal that starts at the J's foot. Whichever way the column fills, the sixth column's third row becomes a major threat.

So the whole triple boils down to one future major threat on the third row — an odd row. That is why the J is counted like a single major odd-row threat: Gray can delay, but one disc at a time cannot defend three cells in two columns. The solver agrees — with Gray to move here, every legal Gray move loses.

Green owns the MIRROR J: foot X1 c5r1, gap c5r2 (Gray O4), upper pair X7 c4r3 + X5 c5r3, hook disc X3 c4r2 — 0-ind (4,0),(4,2),(3,1),(3,2). Anchor row 1 (1-based) ODD. Completing cells run LEFT: C3 = c3r3 (0-ind 2,2), B3 = c2r3 (0-ind 1,2), B4 = c2r4 (0-ind 1,3) — all MINOR (x) on the render, marked claim. Gray has a real gravity-top major threat at c2r1 (0-ind (1,0), renderer 'Major threats: col2 row1 (O) [GT]' — bottom row O6/O8/O2 with the gap at c2r1) — marked td, and the copy makes Green's forced block honest. scr (Green to move): -17 +5 -17 -17 -17 -17 -17 — Green must block the second column and still wins (+5).

coachMessages.text: Same trap, mirrored — and the foot still sits on an odd row. That parity is what turns the J into an endgame squeeze rather than a pretty shape.

legendItems.label: The J's completing cells — now pointing left
Gray's bottom-row threat — Green must block it now

slides.infoProse:
The same J, reflected. The foot sits at the bottom of the fifth column — first row — with the gap above it, and the hook now points left: the fourth column carries the other two green discs. The three completing cells run leftward: the third column's third row, and the second column's third and fourth rows. A mirrored J is every bit as valid as the original.

Now the rule that decides whether any J is real. The pivot cell — the one that eventually becomes the major threat — always lands exactly two rows above the J's bottom disc, so it shares that disc's parity. Lessons 4 to 6 showed who collects which rows when the board fills up at the end of a tight game: Green, who moves first, naturally lands on the odd rows — first, third, fifth — while Gray collects the even ones. So a green J works when the bottom disc of the J sits on an odd row — first, third, or fifth. Here it sits on the first row, and the future major threat ripens on the third row: a row Green collects. Move the identical shape up one row — bottom disc on an even row — and its threat ripens on an even row instead, exactly where Gray naturally lands. Same picture, no squeeze: a ghost.

One honest note about this board: Gray has three discs and a gap on the bottom row, so Green's next move is forced — block the second column. The solver confirms Green blocks and still wins. A J does not demand quiet play; it keeps its grip while the rest of the game goes on.

slides._boardInstructions: Edge-proximity counterexample: slide 1's seven moves shifted two columns right (derived from the verified canonical, solver-verified this task). 7 plies, Gray to move. Green's J intact at F1-F3-G2-G3, 0-ind (5,0),(5,2),(6,1),(6,2), anchor row 1 ODD — the shape and parity are fine; only the geography is wrong. Its three completing cells would sit at H3/I3/I4 — an eighth and ninth column that do not exist (KB false_positives[2], Allen edge-proximity failure). Renderer: 'Major threats: none'; leftover leftward minors only. scr (Gray to move): -6 -5 0 +2 -4 -5 +1 — GRAY to move now WINS (+2 at the fourth column), where the centred J left Gray losing everywhere. Overlays: win rings on the four J discs only; the dead extension cells are off-board so the copy names them instead.

coachMessages.text: Same shape, pressed against the wall — the completing cells fall off the board, and the solver's verdict flips. A J needs room on its open side.

legendItems.label: The same four J discs — against the wall

slides.infoProse:
These are the same seven moves as the first slide, pushed two columns to the right. The J is intact — foot on the sixth column's first row, an odd row, gap above it, hook on the seventh column — and yet the solver's verdict flips completely: with Gray to move, Gray now has a winning line, where the centred version left Gray losing everywhere. Nothing is wrong with the shape. What is missing is room.

The J's punch was its three completing cells extending past the hook. Here they would need an eighth and a ninth column, and the board ends at seven. That is the first failure condition, edge proximity: a J needs two columns of space on its open side. The second is overcutting: the pivot cell just past the hook — on the first slide, the sixth column's third row — belongs to every one of the J's winning lines. If Gray ever owns that cell, the horizontal and the diagonal die together and the triple threat evaporates, so watch what Gray collects on the J's open side. The third is parity cancellation: the J is worth one major odd-row threat, no more — if Gray has built two odd-row threats of its own in separate columns, they outweigh it, and the squeeze the J relies on never arrives.

A J is a strong asset, not a guaranteed win. Before counting on one: check the edge, check the pivot cell, and check the rest of the board's threats.
